source.filename: 2016-Derivation of the exact stiffness matrix of shear-deformable multi-layered beam element in partial interaction.pdf

constitutive_assumptions: Connected members are made of linear elastic, homogeneous, and isotropic materials.
Timoshenko kinematic assumptions are adopted for each layer, where cross-sections remain plane but not orthogonal to the beam axis after deformation.
Relative longitudinal slip is permitted at adjacent layer interfaces through a linear and continuous relationship between interface shear stress and slip (Dsci = ksci * gi).
Discretely located shear connectors are treated as continuously distributed along the beam length.
Transverse displacement v is assumed to be identical for all layers, neglecting transversal separation or uplift between adjacent layers.
Curvature and cross-section rotation are allowed to differ independently across different layers due to independent shear deformations.
Small strain and geometrically linear displacement kinematics are assumed.
External transverse distributed load py applied to the beam element is assumed to be constant along the element length, resulting in a linear total shear force distribution.
control_variables: Layer material properties in numerical examples: Young's modulus E = 8000 MPa (Examples 1 and 2) or E = 50000 MPa (Example 3), and Poisson's ratio nu = 0.3.
Shear correction factor: 5/6 for rectangular sections in Examples 1 and 2; 1.0 in Example 3.
Identical layer width of 0.1 m (or 10 cm) across cross-sections.
Constant layer depths in each benchmark configuration (four 0.2 m layers in Example 1; two 0.2 m outer layers and one 0.4 m core in Example 2; layers of 10 cm, 6 cm, 8 cm, and 4 cm in Example 3).
Applied static loading magnitudes: 100 kN concentrated load (Example 1) or 10 kN/m uniformly distributed load (Examples 2 and 3).
Computing environment for processing time assessment: PC with 3.20 GHz CPU and 8 GB RAM.
dependent_variables: Transverse displacement and mid-span / maximum deflection ratio (Timoshenko vs. Bernoulli models).
Interlayer slip distributions along the beam and end-beam slip values (g1, g2, g3).
Cross-section rotations of individual layers (theta_1, theta_2).
Internal forces and moments (maximum bending moment Mmax, normal force Ni, shear force Ti).
Total computational processing time in seconds across varying element discretizations.

evidence_relevant_to_topic.claim: The governing differential equations for a multi-layered beam with n+1 shear-deformable layers in partial interaction can be formulated in terms of interlayer slips and shear deformations as primary variables, and decoupled analytically via eigenvalue decomposition.

The exact stiffness matrix for a shear-deformable multi-layered beam element with (4n+6) degrees of freedom can be derived in closed form using the direct stiffness method, eliminating locking phenomena and mesh dependence.

Transverse deflection is more significantly affected by cross-sectional shear flexibility than interlayer slip, with the discrepancy between shear-deformable and shear-rigid models diminishing toward unity as span-to-depth ratio increases.
Partial interaction at layer interfaces diminishes the impact of member shear flexibility on overall transverse displacement compared to fully composite interaction.
Interlayer slip values predicted by shear-deformable Timoshenko modeling are not monotonically larger than those predicted by shear-rigid Bernoulli modeling across all layers.
Reformulating integration constants with exponential scaling prevents numerical ill-conditioning in the element stiffness matrix for positive eigenvalues.

independent_variables: Interface shear connector stiffness ksc (ranging from 0.1 MPa to 100000 MPa, including uniform and dissymmetric distributions).
Span-to-depth ratio L/H (ranging from low ratios below 2 up to 20).
Kinematic model formulation (shear-deformable Timoshenko beam model vs. shear-rigid Bernoulli beam model).
Number of finite elements used in discretization (2, 4, 8, 16, 32 elements).
Structural configuration and boundary conditions (simply supported 4-layered beam, two-span continuous 3-layered beam, and two-span continuous dissymmetric 4-layered beam).
limitations_inferred: Physical experimental validation was not performed; verification relies entirely on comparisons with prior analytical/numerical formulations.
Linear elastic interface spring assumptions cannot capture non-linear contact friction, plastic slip, stick-slip transitions, or interface damage.
Geometrically linear kinematics limit direct applicability to structures undergoing large rotations or large deflections typical of soft continuum robots.
Assumption of identical transverse displacement across all layers precludes modeling normal through-thickness stretching, transverse separation, or delamination.
limitations_stated_by_authors: Transverse separation (uplift) of adjacent layers is not considered.
Materials are restricted to linear elastic, homogeneous, and isotropic behavior.
Interface shear connection is assumed to be continuous and linear.
Formulation is limited to geometrically linear elastic behavior.
All layers are constrained to have identical transverse displacement v.
External distributed load py is assumed constant along each element to ensure a linear shear force distribution.
main_results: Derived the closed-form exact stiffness matrix for a shear-deformable multi-layered beam element in partial interaction with independent layer rotations and shear deformations.

Demonstrated that shear-deformable models predict larger deflections than shear-rigid models across all span-to-depth ratios, with the deflection ratio approaching infinity as L/H approaches zero and unity as L/H approaches infinity.
Found that partial interaction attenuates the influence of shear flexibility on transverse beam deflections compared to full composite interaction.
Demonstrated that transverse displacement is more sensitive to shear flexibility than interlayer slip, which approaches asymptotic behavior significantly faster as L/H increases.
Showed that interlayer slips from the shear-deformable formulation are not always larger than those from the shear-rigid model (e.g., intermediate slip g2 is smaller in Timoshenko kinematics).

Obtained close agreement with Sousa's (2013) exact flexibility matrix results for a dissymmetric 4-layered continuous beam (maximum moment 19.0288 kN*m vs. 19.0306 kN*m; slips agreeing to within tenths of a percent).

Verified that the exact stiffness element is locking-free and mesh-independent, requiring only 2 elements for multi-span continuous beams and maintaining execution times under 0.6 seconds up to 32 elements.
modeling_methods: Timoshenko kinematic beam theory applied to individual layers with independent cross-section rotations and shear strains.
Continuous linear shear connection modeling between interface shear flow and interlayer slip.
Equilibrium formulation of differential multi-layer beam elements yielding coupled second-order ordinary differential equations.
Eigenvalue decomposition / diagonalization of system matrix A to uncouple the differential equations for interlayer slips and shear deformations.
Closed-form analytical integration of uncoupled differential equations under linear shear force distributions.
Direct stiffness method to construct the (4n+6) x (4n+6) exact element stiffness matrix and equivalent nodal force vector.
performance_metrics: Mid-span and maximum deflection ratios between shear-deformable (Timoshenko) and shear-rigid (Bernoulli) models.
Interlayer slip ratios (Timoshenko to Bernoulli) at beam ends.
Cross-section rotation ratios (Timoshenko to Bernoulli) at beam ends.
Interlayer slip magnitudes g1, g2, g3 (mm).
Computational processing time (seconds) versus element count.
possible_gap_implications: The closed-form exact stiffness formulation could be extended to account for transverse separation/uplift and normal contact compliance between adjacent layers.
The formulation could serve as a linear foundation or co-rotational base for modeling large-deflection flexible multi-layered continuum structures or variable-stiffness laminates.
Formulation could be expanded to incorporate non-linear interface shear laws, friction, or elastoplastic constituent behavior.
Experimental testing on multi-layered physical specimens is needed to validate predicted slip-shear coupling effects.
paper.research_objective: To derive the exact finite element stiffness matrix from a closed-form solution of the coupled governing differential equations for linear elastic shear-deformable multi-layered beams in partial interaction, incorporating independent layer rotations and shear deformations while preventing numerical ill-conditioning and locking.
paper.research_problem: Most research on beam members in partial interaction is restricted to two-layered beams, with multi-layered beams receiving less attention. Existing multi-layered beam models often assume identical cross-section rotations across all layers despite shear deformation, or suffer from curvature/slip locking when using standard displacement-based finite element shape functions.
paper.title: Derivation of the exact stiffness matrix of shear-deformable multi-layered beam element in partial interaction
